transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-10-05
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees (Redwood): Jenna Park (AE), Ethan Ross (SE), Maya Chen (SE, joined briefly)
Attendees (Customer): Dr. Ana Ruiz (Head of AI), Tom Bianchi (CTO), Leah Kim (Eng Manager), Raj Patel (Security)
Links shared: deck: https://redwood.ai/decks/medflow-intro (redwood), security packet: https://redwood.ai/security/medflow (redwood)

Summary (auto):
High-level discovery for MedFlow Telehealth evaluating Redwood for patient-note summarization, triage assistant, and appointment automation. Primary concerns: PHI handling, VPC/private deployment, context window for long patient histories (16k-64k), multilingual support (Spanish + Portuguese), and tool-calling for EHR reads/writes. Discussed hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs, quantization and latency, and initial pilot steps.

Topics:
- Data classification and PHI handling
- Deployment model: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem)
- Context length needs (long patient history)
- Multilingual: Spanish/Portuguese plus code-switching
- Tool-calling: EHR read, scheduling, structured output and audit logs
- Security: SOC2, KMS, SSO/SAML, audit logs, data residency

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jenna Park: Hey everyone thanks for joining. Quick roll call on the Redwood side, I'm Jenna, AE, and Ethan is our SE. Maya will pop in to demo a quick quantization slide. How about you all?
[00:06] Dr. Ana Ruiz: Hi all, Ana here. I'll kick us off from product.
[00:09] Tom Bianchi: Tom, CTO.
[00:11] Leah Kim: Leah, engineering manager.
[00:13] Raj Patel: Raj, security.
[00:16] Jenna Park: Great, appreciate it. We're here to understand your use cases and constraints — particularly around PHI, context length, and tool calling. Maybe Ana can describe the top two flows you want to operationalize?
[00:25] Dr. Ana Ruiz: Sure. Two main flows: one is patient-note summarization where outpatient visits can be 6–10 pages, plus prior history, meds, labs. We need the model to ingest full history — ideally one shot, we hate chopping it up because you lose cross-visits context. Second is a triage assistant that reads messages and suggests next steps and possible scheduling actions. Both need structured outputs for downstream systems. Also, Spanish patients are about 20% so bilingual handling is required.
[00:46] Ethan Ross: When you say "full history," what's the average token length you're seeing? Is 8k enough, 16k, 32k?
[00:52] Dr. Ana Ruiz: Average visit plus history is around 10k tokens, but for complex chronic patients it spikes to 30k. We were thinking 32k might be the sweet spot, but some legal notes go beyond that.
[01:03] Leah Kim: And for the triage assistant we want sub-second to low hundreds of ms ideally, especially for UI snips. For batch summarization overnight we can accept higher latency. So SLOs differ by flow.
[01:14] Jenna Park: That makes sense — different latency targets. Raj, any security constraints that will push you toward private/dedicated?
[01:20] Raj Patel: PHI retention policy: nothing persisted outside our VPC unencrypted. We need KMS integration, customer-managed keys preferred. Audit logs retained for 7 years. SOC 2 is table stakes, but we also have to do an annual penetration test and attestations. Ideally we want a private deployment but are open to dedicated if we get the right guarantees.
[01:38] Ethan Ross: Quick note: Redwood Private supports a private control plane and on-prem options; Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools in our infra with customer VPC peering and optional customer KMS integration. We can detail the differences in the security packet.
[01:48] Tom Bianchi: Performance-wise are there big differences between hosted vs dedicated? Like will we see 2x latency improvement on dedicated?
[01:55] Ethan Ross: Typically dedicated reduces noisy neighbor variability and lets you pick bigger batch sizes for throughput. For tail latency, dedicated with pinned instances tends to be more stable; we can target single-digit token generation latency improvements depending on model. But the bigger lever is model variant and quantization. For example a 4-bit quantized 32k model on A100s vs a float16 on shared infra will behave differently.
[02:21] Dr. Ana Ruiz: We heard of model hallucinations with quantized weights — is that still a big risk for medical summarization?
[02:27] Maya Chen: (joins) Hi everyone, sorry late, Maya here. Short answer: quantization can change output characteristics but with Redwood Optimize and evals we catch regressions. For summarization we typically recommend closed-book evals and human-in-the-loop checks for the pilot to tune sampling parameters and system prompts.
[02:44] Leah Kim: For multilingual content, do we need separate models per language or can one model handle Spanish/English switching?
[02:51] Ethan Ross: Many open models are multilingual, but performance varies. Some models degrade on medical Spanish. We usually recommend running a small eval corpus in both languages during pilot — Redwood supports eval harnesses and you can pin different model variants for different routes.
[03:06] Raj Patel: About auditability — we need immutable per-request logs and the ability to show which model/version generated a response and what prompt was used. Also, we need function call traces for EHR writes.
[03:18] Jenna Park: Redwood Console has per-route tracing and token-level cost/latency breakdowns, plus request-level metadata including model version and prompt snapshot. For private/dedicated deployments these can be shipped to your logging stack or retained in our secure storage per retention settings.
[03:33] Tom Bianchi: Can you do a quick comparison of model families you typically recommend for medical summarization and tool-calling? We are leaning open models.
[03:41] Ethan Ross: Sure, high level: Llama-family variants are strong baseline; Mistral/Redwood-verified combos can be good for instruction following. For 32k context, there are 32k-context Llama variants and a few opt variants. Anthropic-like family models tend to be safer out of the box but are more expensive. MosaicML and some custom fine-tuned open models can hit a balance. We should run side-by-side evals: accuracy on summaries, hallucination rate, latency, and token cost.
[04:10] Leah Kim: For tool-calling we need function-style structured output — JSON schema strictly validated — and the ability to rollback EHR writes if the confidence is low. Any standard patterns?
[04:20] Maya Chen: Function calling + structured output is supported; Redwood can validate outputs against JSON schema and return a confidence score. For writes we suggest a two-step flow: generate -> validate -> staging write -> human confirm for P0 actions. For lower-risk tasks auto-apply with audit trail.
[04:38] Dr. Ana Ruiz: How does prefix caching or KV cache help with the long histories? We have a lot of repeated sections like medication lists and problem lists.
[04:46] Ethan Ross: KV/prefix caching is effective when past context is reused across requests. Redwood runtime keeps KV cache for decoders across sessions and can materialize deterministic summaries as cached prefixes. That reduces token cost for repeated patterns but you need to design cache keys carefully for privacy.
[05:02] Raj Patel: On encryption: we need in-transit TLS + customer-managed KMS for at-rest. Is HSM supported for key wraps?
[05:10] Ethan Ross: Yes, integrations with common KMS and HSM providers are supported on Private and Dedicated. We'll include specifics in the security packet.
[05:18] Jenna Park: Can we talk timeline and success criteria briefly? What's a good pilot definition?
[05:23] Leah Kim: Pilot ideally in 4 weeks: ingest sample de-identified notes, run baseline summarization against two models, collect accuracy and hallucination metrics, and test tool-calling flows for scheduling. Success is F1 > 0.82 on key extraction and <3% critical hallucination rate.
[05:40] Dr. Ana Ruiz: Also we need multilingual evals and a test for code-switching.
[05:44] Jenna Park: Great. We'll propose a pilot plan in the next two days. Any budget guardrails?
[05:49] Tom Bianchi: We have a small PoC budget, but long-term we need predictable unit economics. If the hosted solution is cheaper per-token but variable, we might still prefer dedicated for predictability.
[06:01] Ethan Ross: Understood. We'll include modeled cost comparisons for your expected volumes and for both low-latency and batch flows.
[06:09] Raj Patel: One more — data residency: some patients in EU; we need EU data residency for those records. Do you support region pinning?
[06:16] Maya Chen: Yes region pinning and routing by policy is supported; for Private you can deploy in your EU cluster or use Redwood Dedicated in an EU region.
[06:23] Leah Kim: Ok can we talk about sample prompts? We'll send 5 canonical prompts after the call. For the triage assistant, we want the model to call back with a structured object for suggested urgency (low/med/high), suggested next action, and optional scheduling slots.
[06:37] Jenna Park: Perfect. We'll include the schema validation example in the follow-up.
[06:41] Tom Bianchi: For the model list, can you recommend one short-list for pilot (3 models)?
[06:46] Ethan Ross: Yes, I'll propose: 1) LlamaX-32k-finetuned-med (open fine-tuned baseline), 2) Mistral-Instruct-32k (good instruction following), 3) Mosaic-Med-quantized-4bit (higher throughput). We'll include estimated latency/cost curves for each.
[07:05] Dr. Ana Ruiz: Do you support dynamic fallbacks if a model is degraded or fails? For example, fallback from 32k to 16k variant or to hosted?
[07:14] Ethan Ross: Yes, Redwood's smart routing supports fallback policies — region/model tier fallbacks and automatic downgrade to compatible variants. You can set thresholds per route.
[07:25] Leah Kim: About logs — can we capture full prompts and deltas for changes? We need traceability for audits.
[07:31] Jenna Park: Yes, request-level prompt snapshots are available with role-based access control on the console. For private deployments you can forward logs to your SIEM.
[07:40] Raj Patel: What's the onboarding time for private? We have an internal compliance window of 8–12 weeks.
[07:46] Ethan Ross: Private on-prem tends to be longer (8–12 weeks), VPC-private shorter if we provide an image and you handle orchestration, or Redwood can do a managed private install which is typically 6–10 weeks depending on approvals. Dedicated is the fastest to get going if you can accept cloud-managed infra — usually 2–4 weeks for reserved capacity.
[08:04] Dr. Ana Ruiz: For the medical domain, do you recommend fine-tuning or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with a vector store?
[08:12] Maya Chen: Both have pros/cons. Fine-tuning reduces hallucinations for specific templates but is heavier lifecycle cost. RAG with a good vector store, retrieval temperature tuning, and a high-quality chunking strategy often gives faster wins for note summarization and allows updating knowledge without retraining.
[08:28] Tom Bianchi: If we go RAG, how do you handle PII/PHI in the index?
[08:33] Ethan Ross: You can keep the vector store in your VPC encrypted with customer keys; Redwood can orchestrate retrieval hooks but you retain control of the index. For hosted scenarios we recommend de-identification or using a private index in your cloud account.
[08:46] Leah Kim: Ok sounds good. Any blockers we should know about?
[08:49] Raj Patel: The main blockers: KMS/HSM compatibility confirmation, contractual SLAs for data deletion and retention, and pen test attestation.
[08:59] Jenna Park: We'll prioritize those in the security packet.
[09:02] Dr. Ana Ruiz: Quick nit — when you talk about token counts, are you advising tokens or characters? We sometimes conflate.
[09:09] Ethan Ross: We use tokens (approx 3/4 of an English word), we'll convert your sample notes to tokens during the pilot to size context.
[09:17] Jenna Park: Alright let's wrap with explicit next steps. We heard: pricing + contract sheet, security packet, pilot plan and sample model shortlist, bench plan. We'll send those by Friday.
[09:29] Tom Bianchi: Sounds good. Also include rough cost model for 100k tokens/day and 1M tokens/day.
[09:35] Leah Kim: And we'll send the five canonical prompts and a sample de-id dataset for the pilot.
[09:41] Jenna Park: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the kickoff once we align on pilot data.
[09:47] Dr. Ana Ruiz: Thanks, talk soon.
[09:49] Meeting ended.

Notes on transcript quality: speaker overlaps and a couple of mis-heard acronyms (e.g., "kay vee" for KV cache) expected. Some proper names of internal model builds are approximated.
